topics.title: SQL Fundamentals
topics.summary: Querying and manipulating relational data — the single most-used skill in data engineering.
keyPoints: SELECT/WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING/ORDER BY, and the logical order of execution
JOIN types: inner, left/right outer, full outer, self-join
Aggregate functions and window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD)
Indexes and how they speed up (or fail to speed up) queries

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and why can't you filter an aggregate with WHERE?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping/aggregation happens, while HAVING filters groups after aggregation, which is why it can reference aggregate functions like COUNT() or SUM() and WHERE cannot. This follows SQL's logical execution order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY, so at the point WHERE executes, aggregate values don't exist yet. If you try to write 'WHERE COUNT(*) > 5' the database will reject it because that aggregate hasn't been computed at that stage.
interviewQA.tip: Reciting the logical execution order (FROM->WHERE->GROUP BY->HAVING->SELECT->ORDER BY) is a strong signal of real SQL understanding.

topics.title: Data Modeling
topics.summary: Structuring data for correctness (OLTP) or query performance (OLAP/analytics).
keyPoints: Normalization (3NF) reduces redundancy for transactional systems
Denormalization / star schema for analytics: fact tables + dimension tables
Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 1/2) for tracking historical changes
Choosing grain: the level of detail a fact table row represents

interviewQA.question: What's a star schema, and why is it preferred over a fully normalized schema for analytics workloads?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A star schema has a central fact table (measurable events, e.g., sales) surrounded by denormalized dimension tables (e.g., customer, product, date) it references via foreign keys, resembling a star shape. It's preferred for analytics because queries typically involve a small number of large joins rather than the many small joins a fully normalized (3NF) schema would require, which is much faster for the large aggregate scans typical of BI/reporting workloads. The trade-off is data redundancy in dimensions and more complex updates, which is acceptable in a read-heavy analytical system but not in a write-heavy transactional one.
interviewQA.tip: Contrast explicitly with OLTP's normalized design to show you understand the trade-off, not just the definition.

topics.title: Python for Data Engineering
topics.summary: Scripting data pipelines and transformations with Python's data ecosystem.
keyPoints: Pandas for in-memory transformation; when it stops scaling (memory limits)
Reading/writing common formats: CSV, JSON, Parquet, Avro
Virtual environments and dependency management for reproducible pipelines
Logging and error handling in long-running batch scripts

interviewQA.question: Why is Parquet generally preferred over CSV for large-scale data pipelines?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Parquet is a columnar storage format, meaning it stores all values of a column together, which allows much better compression (similar values compress well together) and lets query engines read only the columns actually needed rather than scanning entire rows like CSV requires. Parquet also embeds schema and data types directly in the file, avoiding the type-inference and parsing overhead CSV requires, and supports predicate pushdown so filters can skip irrelevant row groups entirely. The trade-off is that Parquet files aren't human-readable and require specific libraries to inspect, unlike plain-text CSV.
interviewQA.tip: Mention predicate pushdown and columnar compression — these are the concrete technical reasons, not just 'it's faster'.

topics.title: ETL/ELT Concepts
topics.summary: The fundamental pattern of moving and transforming data between systems.
keyPoints: ETL (transform before load) vs ELT (load raw, transform in the warehouse)
Batch vs streaming ingestion, and choosing based on latency requirements
Idempotent pipelines: safe to rerun without duplicating or corrupting data
Data quality checks: schema validation, null checks, row-count reconciliation

interviewQA.question: Why have many modern data teams shifted from ETL to ELT?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Modern cloud data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) offer cheap, elastically scalable compute, so it's now practical to load raw data first and transform it inside the warehouse using SQL (ELT) rather than transforming it in a separate processing layer before loading (ETL). This keeps raw, untransformed data available for reprocessing if transformation logic changes or has bugs, and it lets analysts/analytics engineers (via tools like dbt) own transformation logic in SQL without needing a separate ETL engineering pipeline for every change. The trade-off is you need governance around what's 'raw' vs 'modeled' data in the warehouse to avoid a mess.
interviewQA.tip: Mention dbt as the tool that popularized the 'T' living inside the warehouse for ELT.

topics.title: Data Formats (Parquet, Avro, ORC, JSON, CSV)
topics.summary: Choosing the right file format has a huge impact on storage cost and query performance in a data pipeline.
keyPoints: Parquet/ORC are columnar — great for analytical queries that scan few columns over many rows
Avro is row-based and schema-embedded — great for streaming/serialization with schema evolution
CSV/JSON are human-readable but slow and large for big analytical workloads
Columnar formats compress far better because similar values are stored together

interviewQA.question: Why is Parquet generally preferred over CSV for large-scale analytical workloads?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Parquet stores data column-by-column, so a query that only needs 3 of 50 columns can skip reading the rest entirely (column pruning), and similar values compress much better together than row-by-row CSV. It also supports predicate pushdown, letting engines skip whole row-groups that can't match a filter.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that CSV has no embedded schema or types, adding parsing overhead and ambiguity Parquet avoids.

topics.title: Data Structures for Data Engineering
topics.summary: The core in-memory and on-disk structures that make pipelines fast or slow.
keyPoints: Hash maps for fast joins/lookups; sorted structures for range queries and merges
Partitioning splits large datasets by a key (e.g. date) so queries scan less data
Indexes trade write speed and storage for faster reads on specific columns
Understanding Big-O helps you reason about whether a transform will scale to production data volumes

interviewQA.question: Why does partitioning a table by date dramatically speed up a query that filters on a date range?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: With date-based partitioning, each partition is stored as a separate physical unit (folder/file set). A query filtering WHERE date BETWEEN x AND y lets the engine skip reading partitions entirely outside that range (partition pruning), instead of scanning the whole table and filtering row by row afterward.
interviewQA.tip: Give a concrete example: querying 3 days out of 3 years of daily-partitioned data only touches 3 partitions.

topics.title: Big Data with Spark & Hadoop
topics.summary: Distributed processing frameworks for datasets too large for a single machine.
keyPoints: HDFS for distributed storage; Spark as the dominant distributed compute engine
RDDs vs DataFrames vs Datasets, and Spark's lazy evaluation via DAGs
Partitioning and shuffling — the main cost driver in distributed jobs
Spark's in-memory computation vs Hadoop MapReduce's disk-based model

interviewQA.question: Why is a 'shuffle' operation expensive in Spark, and how would you minimize it?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A shuffle occurs when data needs to be redistributed across partitions/nodes, such as during groupBy, join, or repartition operations — it requires writing intermediate data to disk and transferring it across the network between executors, which is far slower than in-partition ('narrow') transformations like map or filter. To minimize shuffles, you can pre-partition data by the join/group key so related data is already co-located, use broadcast joins for joining a large table with a small one (avoiding a shuffle of the large table entirely), and combine operations to reduce the number of shuffle stages in the DAG.
interviewQA.tip: Mention broadcast joins explicitly — a concrete, high-value optimization technique.

topics.title: Data Warehousing
topics.summary: Designing and operating centralized analytical stores like Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift.
keyPoints: MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) architecture and columnar storage
Clustering/partitioning keys to prune scanned data and control cost
Materialized views for precomputing expensive aggregations
Separation of storage and compute (modern cloud warehouses) for elastic scaling

interviewQA.question: How does partitioning a large table in a cloud data warehouse (e.g., BigQuery) improve both performance and cost?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Partitioning splits a large table into segments (often by date) so that a query with a filter on the partition column only needs to scan the relevant partitions instead of the entire table — this is called partition pruning. Since many cloud warehouses (like BigQuery) charge based on bytes scanned, pruning directly reduces both query cost and latency, sometimes turning a full-table scan of terabytes into a scan of just a few gigabytes for a single day's data. Combining partitioning with clustering on a frequently filtered column compounds these savings further.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that BigQuery-style warehouses bill by bytes scanned — ties performance directly to cost.

topics.title: Workflow Orchestration (Airflow)
topics.summary: Scheduling, sequencing, and monitoring complex data pipelines as directed acyclic graphs.
keyPoints: DAGs, tasks, and operators define pipeline structure and dependencies
Scheduling intervals, backfilling, and catchup behavior
Retries, SLAs, and alerting on task failure
Sensors for waiting on external conditions (e.g., a file arriving in S3)

interviewQA.question: In Airflow, what's the difference between a task failing and a task retrying, and how would you design a pipeline to be resilient to transient failures?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Airflow lets you configure a number of retries with a delay (often exponential backoff) per task, so a task that fails due to a transient issue (a brief network blip, a temporarily overloaded API) automatically retries before being marked as truly failed and triggering alerts or downstream blocking. For this to be safe, each task must be idempotent — rerunning it should produce the same end state rather than duplicating data — which usually means using upsert/merge logic instead of blind inserts, or writing to a staging location before an atomic final swap. Without idempotency, retries can silently create duplicate or corrupted data instead of fixing the problem.
interviewQA.tip: Idempotency is the key word here — retries are only safe if the task is idempotent.

topics.title: Streaming Data with Kafka
topics.summary: Building real-time data pipelines with a distributed, durable event streaming platform.
keyPoints: Topics, partitions, producers, consumers, and consumer groups
Offsets and at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery semantics
Retention: messages persist for a configured period, enabling replay
Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams for integration and stream processing

interviewQA.question: How does Kafka achieve horizontal scalability for consumers, and what happens if you have more consumers than partitions?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Within a consumer group, each partition of a topic is assigned to exactly one consumer at a time, so adding more consumers (up to the number of partitions) increases parallel processing throughput, since each consumer independently processes its assigned partitions. If you have more consumers in a group than partitions, the extra consumers sit idle with no partitions assigned, since a partition can't be split across multiple consumers within the same group — the fix is to increase the topic's partition count if you need more parallelism than the current partition count allows.
interviewQA.tip: Be precise: partitions are the real unit of parallelism, not consumers themselves.

topics.title: dbt & Data Transformation
topics.summary: Managing SQL transformations as version-controlled, tested, documented code instead of ad-hoc scripts.
keyPoints: dbt models are just SELECT statements; dbt handles dependency ordering and materialization (view/table/incremental)
ref() and source() build an explicit DAG of dependencies between models
Built-in tests (unique, not_null, relationships) catch data quality issues automatically
dbt docs auto-generates a lineage graph and documentation from the project

interviewQA.question: What does the 'ref()' function do in dbt, and why is it better than hardcoding table names?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: ref('other_model') tells dbt this model depends on another model, letting dbt automatically build the correct execution order (a DAG) and swap in the right fully-qualified table name per environment (dev/staging/prod). Hardcoding a table name breaks across environments and loses that dependency tracking entirely.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that ref() is also what powers dbt's auto-generated lineage graph in its docs.

topics.title: NoSQL Databases for Engineers
topics.summary: Choosing the right non-relational store for a workload, and understanding the tradeoffs vs SQL.
keyPoints: Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j) — pick by access pattern
CAP theorem: under a network partition you trade off consistency vs availability
Denormalization is common in NoSQL — design the schema around your queries, not entities
Eventual consistency means a read right after a write may not reflect it yet, in some of these stores

interviewQA.question: When would you choose Cassandra (wide-column) over a relational database for a workload?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Cassandra is a strong fit for very write-heavy, high-volume workloads (e.g. IoT sensor data, event logs) that need to scale horizontally across many nodes with high availability and can tolerate eventual consistency, where a single relational database would become a write bottleneck.
interviewQA.tip: Contrast with a use case needing strong transactional consistency (e.g. banking), where relational is still the better fit.

topics.title: Data Lake & Lakehouse Architecture
topics.summary: Storing raw and structured data at scale, and the modern lakehouse pattern combining lake flexibility with warehouse reliability.
keyPoints: Data lake: cheap object storage (S3/ADLS/GCS) holding raw data of any format
Lakehouse (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi): adds ACID transactions and schema enforcement on top of a lake
Medallion architecture: bronze (raw) -> silver (cleaned) -> gold (business-ready) layers
Table formats solve the 'small files problem' and enable time travel/versioning

interviewQA.question: What problem does a table format like Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg solve that a plain data lake on S3 doesn't?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A plain data lake (raw files in S3) has no built-in concept of transactions, so concurrent writes can produce partial/corrupted reads, there's no easy way to enforce or evolve schema, and deleting or updating records means rewriting entire files. Table formats like Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg add a transaction log on top of the raw files that provides ACID guarantees, schema enforcement and safe evolution, efficient upserts/deletes (MERGE), and 'time travel' to query historical table versions — essentially bringing data-warehouse reliability to lake storage, which is the core idea behind the 'lakehouse' pattern.
interviewQA.tip: Naming the transaction log mechanism (Delta log / Iceberg metadata) shows real depth beyond buzzwords.

topics.title: ML Ops Pipelines
topics.summary: Operationalizing machine learning models: from training to deployment to monitoring.
keyPoints: Feature stores for consistent features between training and serving
Model versioning and experiment tracking (MLflow)
CI/CD for ML: automated retraining and validation pipelines
Monitoring for data drift and model performance decay in production

interviewQA.question: What is 'training-serving skew' in ML Ops, and how does a feature store help prevent it?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Training-serving skew happens when the features computed during model training (often batch-processed from historical data) differ subtly from the features computed at inference time in production (often computed differently, in real time, by different code), causing the model to underperform in production despite strong training metrics. A feature store centralizes feature definitions and computation logic in one place, serving the exact same feature values (or logically identical pipelines) to both offline training jobs and online real-time inference, eliminating the duplicated, divergent logic that causes skew.
interviewQA.tip: The key insight interviewers want: skew comes from duplicated feature logic, and a feature store centralizes it.

topics.title: Distributed Systems for Data
topics.summary: The theoretical and practical foundations underlying scalable, fault-tolerant data infrastructure.
keyPoints: CAP theorem: consistency, availability, partition tolerance trade-offs
Data replication strategies and how they affect consistency guarantees
Exactly-once vs at-least-once processing semantics in stream processing
Backpressure and how streaming systems handle producers outpacing consumers

interviewQA.question: In a distributed streaming pipeline, how can you achieve effectively 'exactly-once' processing when the underlying delivery is only at-least-once?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: True exactly-once delivery across a network is famously difficult (impossible to fully guarantee end-to-end), so most systems instead achieve 'effectively exactly-once' processing by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes on the consumer side — for example, using a unique message ID as a deduplication key so reprocessing the same message twice doesn't double-count it. This is often paired with checkpointing (tracking the last successfully processed offset) so that after a failure, processing resumes from a known-safe point and only reprocesses a small, bounded window of messages, which idempotent writes then handle safely.
interviewQA.tip: Say explicitly that true exactly-once is theoretically hard — 'effectively exactly-once via idempotency' is the real-world answer.

topics.title: Data Governance & Quality
topics.summary: Ensuring data is trustworthy, discoverable, secure, and compliant at organizational scale.
keyPoints: Data lineage: tracking where data comes from and how it's transformed
Data catalogs for discoverability and documentation (metadata management)
Automated data quality testing (e.g., Great Expectations, dbt tests)
Access control, PII handling, and regulatory compliance (GDPR, data masking)

interviewQA.question: How would you design automated data quality checks for a critical daily pipeline, and what should happen when a check fails?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Layer checks at multiple levels: schema validation (correct types/columns), null and uniqueness constraints on key fields, referential integrity against dimension tables, and statistical/anomaly checks (e.g., row count or key metric shouldn't deviate more than X% from the trailing average) to catch subtler issues a rigid schema check would miss. When a critical check fails, the pipeline should halt before publishing bad data downstream (a 'circuit breaker' pattern) rather than silently loading it, alert the owning team with enough context to debug quickly, and ideally quarantine the bad batch for inspection rather than discarding it outright.
interviewQA.tip: The 'halt before publishing, don't silently proceed' principle is the core answer interviewers want.

topics.title: Real-Time Analytics & OLAP
topics.summary: Serving sub-second analytical queries over huge, constantly-updating datasets.
keyPoints: OLAP engines (ClickHouse, Druid, Pinot) are optimized for fast aggregations over large datasets
Pre-aggregation and materialized views trade storage/compute for query speed
Real-time ingestion pipelines (Kafka -> OLAP store) keep dashboards near-live
Star schema / denormalized wide tables reduce expensive joins at query time

interviewQA.question: Why can't you just point a real-time dashboard at your regular OLTP (transactional) database?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: An OLTP database is optimized for many small, fast reads/writes of individual rows (e.g. one order), not large aggregation scans across millions of rows — running heavy analytical queries against it competes for resources with production transactions and is far slower than a purpose-built OLAP engine designed for that access pattern.
interviewQA.tip: Mention CDC (change data capture) as the common bridge to stream OLTP changes into an OLAP store.

topics.title: Cost Optimization & Data Platform Scaling
topics.summary: Keeping a growing data platform performant without an unbounded cloud bill.
keyPoints: Right-size compute clusters (auto-scaling, spot instances for batch jobs) instead of over-provisioning
Lifecycle policies move cold data to cheaper storage tiers automatically
Query cost awareness — a poorly written query can scan terabytes unnecessarily
Monitor cost per pipeline/team so growth is visible before it becomes a crisis

interviewQA.question: A monthly cloud data-warehouse bill has tripled with no proportional increase in data volume. How would you investigate?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Check for queries doing full table scans that could use partition pruning or clustering, look for jobs re-processing the same data repeatedly (missing incremental logic), review recently added dashboards/BI tools that might be firing expensive ad-hoc queries, and break down cost by team/pipeline to isolate the source before optimizing.
interviewQA.tip: Mention query cost estimation tools (e.g. BigQuery's dry-run) as a proactive prevention measure.

codingModule.focus: Coding exercises centered on SQL fluency and large-scale data processing rather than classic interview DSA.
topics: Advanced SQL problems (window functions, multi-way joins, CTEs, deduplication logic)
PySpark/Pandas data transformation problems (groupBy, aggregations, schema handling)
ETL pipeline debugging exercises (fixing broken DAGs, handling late-arriving data)
Partitioning & hashing strategies for large-scale processing
Working with semi-structured data (JSON/Parquet parsing, schema evolution)
Streaming coding exercises (windowing logic with Spark Structured Streaming / Kafka consumers)
Data quality & validation scripting (writing assertions, anomaly detection)

systemDesignModule.focus: System design scenarios centered on moving, storing, and governing data at scale.
topics: Design a Data Warehouse / Lakehouse architecture (star schema vs data vault, partitioning strategy)
Design a Real-time Streaming Pipeline (Kafka → Spark/Flink → sink, exactly-once semantics)
Design a Batch ETL Orchestration system (Airflow DAG design, dependency management, backfills)
Design a Data Lake with governance (schema registry, access control, data catalog)
Design a Change Data Capture (CDC) pipeline (Debezium-style, handling schema drift)
Design a Feature Store for ML pipelines
Design a Data Pipeline Monitoring & Alerting system (freshness SLAs, volume anomaly detection)

behavioralModule.focus: Scenarios around pipeline ownership, upstream/downstream dependencies, and data trust across teams.
topics: Describe a time a pipeline failure broke a critical downstream dashboard or report
How have you handled an unclear or undocumented data contract from an upstream team
Tell me about prioritizing a broken ETL fix against a new feature request
Describe collaborating with data scientists/analysts on a data quality dispute
How did you handle a large schema-change or migration project with minimal downtime
Tell me about a time stakeholders lost trust in a dataset and how you rebuilt it
Describe pushing back on a request for data you knew was not production-ready
